# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):

- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").

- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: Marcus walked away from extra paperwork and monthly transfers, which is the simplicity-over-yield point the group names, so leaving him on his own is one odd placement; Aisha's point is about insurance and being easy to explain, which only loosely fits a name that leads with cash access.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three are about what would have made a difference to where the cash sits.

founder.order_why: Context, problem, solution and launch run in a sensible order, but screens 21 and 22 (how finance leads answer, who gets a link) sit under an INTERVIEWS · SENT kicker, so I'm choosing who receives the study after it is apparently already sent.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so the context step reads as asked twice.
founder.missing: Nothing asks my price (a flat 0.25% annual fee on the balance, against the 0.15–0.60% the bank's treasury takes), what the status quo costs a startup in yield given up, the small first step I'd ask for (start with part of the reserve and grow it), or who signs off on moving the reserve (the founder-CEO, sometimes the board or a tax adviser) versus the finance lead who moves cash monthly. Relative advantage also gets no 'what do you believe' screen, unlike compatibility and adoption friction.

PRIMARY.order_why: It moves from whether I fit, to my recent experience, to the idea, and each follow-up comes right after the answer it asks about.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked what we actually earn now (about 3.2% in the bank's treasury sweep) or how much of the raise sits in reserve. It also didn't ask about the ongoing operational burden of running a second provider, or whether I'd trust Palus as safe, and those matter more to me than yield. And it didn't ask who else (CEO, board) has to sign off on moving the reserve.

screens.why7: It is an ability with the right four-plus-escape scale, and it can go either way, but the belief is shown with a doubled subject and the two bar lines disagree ('only with help or approval' beside the list against 'only sometimes' in the box).
screens.instead: Keel will test: Most finance leads could wait one to two business days for their long-term cash. Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say 'Only sometimes' or 'No'. Also replace the Plaid row with 'They could keep their current bank account'.

screens.why1: Right after saying how Palus fits what finance leads already do, asking what it does better than the bank's treasury product is the obvious next question for me as the founder.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to me, but the belief's 'their last cash decision' is not how I or a finance lead would name the monthly move from treasury to checking, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: What Palus beats Mercury or Brex Treasury on is exactly what I pitch every day, so I can answer it from my own numbers.
screens.why4: A free box for up to four lines with a 9-word limit fits a benefit list, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right escape for a founder who can't name one.
screens.why5: The belief carries my words 'higher yield without hiring for treasury' unchanged.
screens.why7: My one row bundles two gains (more yield, no treasury hire) and Keel neither splits it nor flags that 'without hiring' is something the bank's treasury already gives today, and the belief's occasion 'cash decision' is the ambiguous kind the card warns of.
screens.instead: Same question, but split my line into rows 'More yield on cash we won't touch for months' and 'No switching banks to get it', flag 'without hiring for treasury' as something the bank treasury already gives, and word the occasion as 'their last monthly move of reserve cash'.

screens.why1: Right after I said what Palus does better than today's way, Keel shows me the benefit back and the belief it will test, which is exactly where this check belongs.
screens.why2: 'Higher yield' and 'hiring for treasury' are plain to me, but 'their last cash decision' is vague and makes me re-read: is it the monthly sweep, or where the raise sits?
screens.why3: I know my own claim and my customers' situation, so I can judge whether this row and belief say what I mean.
screens.why4: The single row bundles two gains, more yield and no treasury hire, that a stranger could get one without the other, so it should be two rows.
screens.why5: The row is my own label word for word, and the belief carries it unchanged.
screens.why7: The belief keeps my only benefit and the stranger's fixed four with the escape are intact, but the row bundles two gains and the occasion 'cash decision' is the ambiguous word the card warns about, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Rows: 'More yield on the raise's reserve' · 'No treasury hire or extra ops time'; belief: 'For most, with it, the last time they decided where the raise's cash sits would have given them more yield on the reserve and no treasury hire or extra ops time.'

screens.why1: After compatibility and relative advantage, asking what a finance lead must do to start using Palus is the obvious next question in the solution step.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps and learning are plain to me, and the 9-word limit per effort is clear enough to type 'Link the company bank account through Plaid' without a second read.
screens.why3: I know what onboarding asks of a finance lead: connect the bank via Plaid, then move the long-term reserve and set the transfer rules, so I can answer from my own product.
screens.why4: The only option on this box is the escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right way out for a founder who isn't sure what onboarding asks.
screens.why5: The belief repeats my second effort word for word, 'move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury', with their voice kept and nothing reworded.
screens.why7: Both rows are one-effort, base-form steps the finance lead takes, but the effort set as the belief, moving the reserve, is close to the founder's call on where cash sits (Purchase friction's ground) and to the switch itself, so a finance lead's No may mean 'not my decision' rather than 'too much effort'; the Plaid link is the cleaner adoption effort.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it? -> 'Link the company bank account through Plaid; Set a rule for when cash moves back to the bank', belief: Most would link the company bank account through Plaid.

screens.why1: It follows straight from screen 16, where I said what they'd have to do to start, so checking Keel's rows of those efforts is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are everyday words to a startup finance lead banking with Mercury or Brex.
screens.why3: Linking the account and moving the reserve are things the finance lead does with their own hands every cash decision.
screens.why4: Both rows are distinct and in my words, but the new monthly habit my product asks for is missing: setting the rule for when cash comes back to the bank.
screens.why5: Both rows are mine: the Plaid connection from my launch post and moving the reserve out of the bundled treasury, which is the problem I named.
screens.why7: The tested effort is something the finance lead does, but moving the reserve is close to the buy itself, and at a funded startup the founder-CEO signs where the reserve sits, so it leans on Purchase friction's ground; Link the company bank account through Plaid is the cleaner step.
screens.instead: Rows: Link the company bank account through Plaid; Set a rule for when cash returns to the bank; Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury. Belief: Most would link the company bank account through Plaid.

screens.why1: After I listed the efforts on the screens before, picking the one most likely to stop a finance lead is the obvious next step before strangers get one question.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury (Mercury Treasury, Brex Treasury) are everyday words to a startup finance lead, and the title reads on first pass.
screens.why3: Linking the bank account and moving the reserve are things the finance lead does themselves in the bank dashboard, so they can answer from their own work.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct, both mine, in my words, and a short pick list needs no chip on the founder's side.
screens.why5: Both rows are exactly what I typed, and the belief keeps my words 'Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury' unreworded.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form steps the finance lead takes themselves, with no sign-off, in order and with no suggestion slipped in, and the belief can go either way; but moving the reserve sits close to the decision to put money in at all (where the cash sits) rather than the effort of starting, so the measure bends toward Purchase friction and Commitment.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? · Link the company bank account through Plaid · Set a rule to move cash back when the bank balance falls low · Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury

screens.why1: Asking whether to offer a pilot just before the study goes out is the obvious place for it, and as a founder who wants batchmates to sign up I see why it is here.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with a hint that shows the exact line respondents see is plain to me on first reading.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups from the people I survey is my own call about my own launch.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for a binary choice, and there is no escape chip because none is needed.
screens.why5: My pick, Yes, is kept, and the line shown to respondents ("Would you try this for real? Leave your email.") does not leak my product name or roles.

screens.why1: Picking the interviewer's voice just before sending is the natural last setup step, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'records the voice you pick once' and '400 credits, whichever you choose' need a second read to see that the cost doesn't depend on the choice, and the question says 'who' while the hint talks of a voice and the typed answer of a face.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which voice my finance leads would take seriously after hearing a 5-second sample.
screens.why4: Two voices are distinct and hearable, but there is no visible sign of what differs between them (tone, accent, face) beyond the name, so the choice is near-blind until played.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study; it addresses my respondents as finance leads, as I typed.
screens.instead: Which voice should ask finance leads your questions? (Daphne, picked for you / Saskia) — tap to hear each; it costs 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Right before sending, choosing how finance leads will take the interview is the obvious last setup step after picking who asks the questions.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, let them choose are plain to a founder who built a 'two buttons and a giant number' product; each option says what the respondent actually does.
screens.why3: I know my finance leads are busy people working in Slack and banking dashboards, so I can judge whether they'd rather tap through or talk to a video interviewer.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete choices covering voice, text and both, with no overlap and nothing missing for this decision.
screens.why5: It keeps my actor ('finance leads') and my pick 'Read and tap' is offered as typed, with nothing of the product leaking.

screens.why1: After choosing how finance leads answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words a founder reads at once; 'Contacts page' and 'open link' are Keel's own terms but explained in the line under each.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to batchmates and finance leads I know by name or posting in a founder group, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three cover named, searched and open-group sending, but the study needs both finance leads and founders and nothing lets me send different people to the two parts, so a mixed send (batchmates by name plus a post in a YC or finance-lead group) has no option.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea or roles is changed here; it's a sending choice and my pick of people I know by name is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? (pick any): People I know by name (each their own link) / People I found with Keel (a Contacts list) / A group, with one open link (e.g. a YC batch or finance-leads Slack) -- and for each, whether they're finance leads or founders.

screens.why_b1: The headline says 'Not holding up' and gives Relative advantage's 2 of 6 beside it, but the screen says the verdict is the worst card, and Adoption friction 'Did not hold' at 3 of 7 against a bar of 5 looks worse, so I cannot tell which card actually decides it.
screens.why_b2: Compatibility and Relative advantage read cleanly as count against bar, but Adoption friction says '3 yes (1 on a condition)', then '3 of 7 would do it', then '2 short · 1 on a condition', and I had to read it twice to see whether the conditional yes counts and what '2 short' means.
screens.why_b3: All three dimension names and belief lines are word for word the ones I checked, even though Keel's statement of my solution above them is garbled ('the finance lead the treasury account links...', 'gets back the cash back').
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what this means for Palus, for example that finance leads accept the two-day wait but few see a better outcome or would move the reserve, or what I should test or change next.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but seven finance leads is a small sample the page never flags, and 'not holding' beside 'did not hold' blurs which result is firmer.
screens.instead: Not holding up, decided by Adoption friction: only 3 of 7 would move the reserve out of the bank's treasury (bar 5), and only 2 of 6 saw a better outcome, though 6 of 7 can wait two days, so liquidity isn't the blocker; find out what keeps the reserve at the bank before pushing yield, and treat 7 people as an early read.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 6 of 7 for against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know my two-day liquidity belief held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, the rule line says which count for me, and the strip puts the marker at 5 with 6 for and 1 against, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: "Compatibility" and "Most finance leads could wait two days for their cash" are exactly what I checked on the way in, and the question keeps my two days.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me concretely that liquidity timing is not my blocker and points me to the dimension that is, so I know where to look next.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and "a lean, not a call" is said, but the So line flatly says the two-day wait "is not what will stop them" when half the yeses were only "most of the time", and it names Adoption friction as the blocker with nothing on this card to back it.
screens.instead: Say half of the yeses were only 'most of the time', so keep a same-day buffer in the bank with the auto-transfer rule; and say Adoption friction 'looks like' the blocker rather than stating it is.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits right beside 2 of 6 said it would have gone better, and the So line ties 4 of 6 no difference to my limit of 2, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Better 2 and Same 4 over 6 read at once, but 'bar 4 of 6' is a count of people for me while the 4 next to it is a count against, so I had to read the bracket to see the marker is my target and not where the against bar stops.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and 'higher yield without hiring for treasury' on my last cash decision are exactly the belief I checked, and the question says Palus and my job in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me I'm past my limit and points to reasons, but it doesn't say what the quotes show: the ones who saw no difference rank ease of getting cash back, no new paperwork and insured safety above yield, so higher yield alone won't make them switch.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 with 6 counted stays visible, Rachel's I can't tell is set apart, and it calls itself a small group, a lean not a call, and a hypothetical, with nothing claimed past these six.
screens.instead: Not holding up: 2 of 6 said a lot better, 4 said no difference (you needed at least 4 better); the four who saw no difference put fast access, no extra paperwork and insured safety ahead of yield, so lead with that, not the rate.

screens.why_b1: Did not hold sits right beside 3 of 7 would do it, bar 5 of 7, 2 short, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, the strip shows 3 for and 4 against, and the marker sits at 5 of 7 with the one-in-three rule beside it; all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury' are exactly the effort and belief I picked.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count; it switches to a 'bar of 2' against when the card's bar is 5 of 7 for. It promises 'their reasons are below' but shows one quote, and it never says what to change: Aisha's payroll condition and the tax and safety worries point to keeping operating cash in the bank and starting with a small slice.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the card says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would not move the reserve (bar: at most 2 against); the catch is payroll reach and tax or safety, so pitch leaving payroll cash at the bank and moving only a small slice first.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its status word with the deciding count and bar beside it (2 of 6 vs bar 4 of 6, 3 of 7 vs bar 5 of 7, 6 of 7 vs bar 5 of 7), and the against counts agree with them, though 'Not holding up' and 'Did not hold' are two words for what reads as the same verdict.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are exactly the ones I checked, including my own 'higher yield without hiring for treasury' label.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what these answers mean for Palus; the theme 'Easy cash access and simplicity over yield' hints that yield is the wrong lead, but I have to draw that myself.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and nothing is overclaimed, but the count lines mislead: Lena is 'never saw it' on Relative advantage while her why sits on Compatibility, Dana, Marcus and Aisha 'never saw' Adoption friction though they answered a why elsewhere, and Lena's board-and-insurance quote is filed as the one Compatibility no even though it is not about a two-day wait.
screens.why_b6: The quotes reframe my pitch: 'nobody asks why we earned a bit less, they'd ask why we lost any', a better rate inside the bank they already use, treasury that pays monthly bills so two-click access beats a point of yield, and a board that only cares that the money is insured all go past the yield-and-fee story I typed.

screens.why1: As the first screen it's a gate, and checking whether I'm at a startup banking with Mercury or Brex is an obvious place to start.
screens.why2: Mercury, Brex and 'startup bank' are everyday words for me, so I can answer instantly.
screens.why3: I know exactly where our company banks because I run those accounts every day.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it completely for a gate, and a gate takes no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the screen drops part of the founder's segment: it doesn't ask about a raise in the last two years or whether I'm the one who handles the cash, so an engineer at any Mercury customer would pass.
screens.why6: It's one short question with two options and nothing that only reads on a page, so I'd hear it once and answer.
screens.instead: Do you look after the bank accounts at a startup that raised money in the last two years and banks with Mercury, Brex or similar? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after confirming I bank with Mercury or similar, asking whether my raise cash earned less than it could have is an obvious first question about how we hold that money.
screens.why2: Treasury rates is my trade's word, but 'did you find cash earning below' reads oddly, and it doesn't say which cash or which Treasury rate (T-bills? which tenor?), so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I know what our accounts yield (about 3.2%) and roughly where T-bills sit, so I can answer from what I see every month.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete for a gate, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: Benchmarking against Treasury rates tips me off that someone is selling yield, a small hint at the product, though it names nothing.
screens.why6: One short sentence then 'Yes or no.' is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: It is one act in the window and the shape is right, but almost every startup keeps operating cash in checking earning well below Treasury rates, so nearly everyone like me says Yes and No is left to very few, close to a gate on the circumstance.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did cash from your raise that you weren't about to spend earn less than Treasury bills were paying? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether our raise cash earned below Treasury rates, showing me a product that claims to beat that is the obvious next step before part 2.
screens.why2: Plaid, custodian, short-duration, floating-rate, government-backed mortgage bonds and money market fund fees are all words I use running our cash, so I follow it on first read.
screens.why3: Where our reserve sits, what it earns, and how fast it gets back to checking is exactly what I decide and watch.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It reads as an idea shown on purpose, framed as what the builders believe, and nothing of their plan or their names for people leaks beyond the product itself.
screens.why6: Heard once, it runs long: it says 'holds your long-term reserve in ... mortgage bonds' twice and stacks four short claims, and 'a fee of 0.15 to 0.60 percent' is a mouthful at the end; it can be said, but I'd struggle to hold it all.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account that holds your long-term reserve in short-duration, government-backed mortgage bonds. It links to your bank through Plaid, a regulated custodian holds the bonds in your company's name, and cash is back in checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent a year, more than a money market fund earns after its fee.

screens.why1: Right after the Palus card, asking whether I could live with a delay getting money out of a reserve is the obvious first thing to check.
screens.why2: "Your last cash decision" is vague to me (a wire, a sweep, moving money into T-bills?), and "waited two days for your cash" doesn't say whose cash or where it was coming from, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know when we've needed money out fast, but tying it to one fuzzy "cash decision" and an unstated source means I'd partly guess.
screens.why4: "Yes, most of the time" and "Only sometimes" don't fit a single past occasion; for one moment I either could have waited or couldn't.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks beyond the idea card, but "two days" reads like the condition got clipped (one to two business days, for money coming out of the reserve) and lost its object.
screens.why6: Heard once it's short, one question, four options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: It's on one measure, with the escape present and a balance that could go either way, but the ability scale's frequency rungs bend against a single last occasion, and the condition drops its qualifier and object (one to two business days to pull cash out of the reserve), a pitfall the card names.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you needed to move money out of your reserve. Could you have waited one to two business days for it to arrive? Yes, easily · Yes, with some planning · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the can-I-wait question, asking whether Palus would have beaten what I did with our raise cash is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: 'Cash decision' makes me stop and think, because I make cash decisions every day (paying vendors, approving payroll), and the question doesn't say it means where we parked the raise money.
screens.why3: I know exactly what we did with our reserve, which is mostly a money market sweep at about 3.2% with no operational overhead, so I can judge whether this would have been better.
screens.why4: The four rungs are distinct and complete, 'Worse' is a real answer for me since I care more about low operational burden than extra yield, and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The only product detail I see is the idea card shown on purpose, and 'keep the money from a raise safe and earning' is plain enough for me to read as my own job.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is two short sentences and four short options I can hold, with the escape said last.
screens.why7: The four fixed answers and the escape are right, but the occasion uses 'cash decision', the ambiguous word the card names as a pitfall, and the stem drops '{Name}, {what it is}' after Palus.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you decided where to park cash from your raise. Would Palus, a treasury account in government-backed mortgage bonds, have done that better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: I just said Palus wouldn't change much, so asking what would help is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It plays back what I picked in words I'd use and asks one clear thing, though 'keeping raise money earning' is a little clunky.
screens.why3: I run our cash day to day, so I know what would make it better for us, which is mostly less operational hassle rather than more yield.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: The job was keeping the money safe and earning, and dropping 'safe' tilts the question toward yield, which isn't my priority.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question and nothing that only the eye reads, so it is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said Palus wouldn't make much difference on your last cash decision. What would make looking after your raise money easier or safer for you, if anything?

screens.why1: After asking whether Palus would have done my last cash decision better, asking whether I'd actually move the reserve to use it is the obvious closing question.
screens.why2: Long-term reserve and my bank's treasury are what I call them, since I already sweep cash into Mercury's treasury at about 3.2%, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Moving the reserve is my own call and my own work, and I know exactly what it would cost me in hassle.
screens.why4: Yes, a real condition, probably not and no cover it, and the payroll condition is the actual catch for someone like me, even if a long-term reserve isn't usually what payroll draws on.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose, and the step is put in words a finance lead uses.
screens.why6: One short question, four short options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The effort is one I take myself, the options are on the one measure of whether I'd take it, two count for and two against, the condition is mine and not true of every step, and I can't tell sits apart.

screens.why1: I just said I wouldn't move the reserve, so asking why comes right after that answer.
screens.why2: It doesn't say back what I answered; it assumes my reason was trouble, and I'd say 'our reserve' or 'the treasury balance' before 'long-term reserve'.
screens.why3: Why we keep cash where it is is something I decide every week, and the operational burden is exactly my reason.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: Calling my 'no' 'too much trouble' puts a reason in my mouth I never gave; it might be risk, or the board, or the yield isn't worth it.
screens.why6: One short question that is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said you wouldn't move your reserve out of your bank's treasury. What holds you back, if anything?
